'''Johann Andreas von Segner''' ({{langx|hu|Segner János András}}, {{langx|de|Johann Andreas von Segner}}, {{langx|sk|Ján Andrej Segner}}, {{langx|la|Iohannes Andreas de Segner}}; October 9, 1704 &ndash; October 5, 1777) was a [[Kingdom of Hungary|Hungarian]] scientist of German descent. He was born in the [[Kingdom of Hungary]], in the former Hungarian capital city of Pozsony, or Pressburg (today [[Bratislava]]).

==Early life and education==
Johann Segner was born to Johann Michael von Segner and his wife Christine von Segner (née Fischer) on probably the 10 October 1704.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Kleinert |first=Andreas |last2=Steiner |first2=Thomas |date=2018 |title=Leonhard Euler Briefwechsel |url=https://edoc.unibas.ch/68192/1/20190110134703_5c373ec770239.pdf |website=Birkhäuser Verlag |page=233}}</ref> Other sources mention also the 4 or the 9 October.<ref name=":0" /> His father was a tax clerk. His paternal ancestors came from [[Styria]] to Pressburg<ref>[http://www-groups.dcs.st-and.ac.uk/~history/Biographies/Segner.html Segner biography<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> in the [[History of Hungary 1700-1919|Kingdom of Hungary]]; by the 18th century. In 1596 the family was granted nobility for their military accomplishments by [[Rudolf II, Holy Roman Emperor|Rudolph II]].<ref name=":0" /> He studied at Pressburg and [[Debrecen]]. In April 1725, Segner began studying at the [[University of Jena]].<ref name=":0" /> Under the guidance of [[Georg Erhard Hamberger]], Segner developed an evidence for the [[Descartes' rule of signs|cartesian rule of signs]].<ref name=":0" /> In his third year at Jena, he began to teach other students in mathematics.<ref>Kleinert, Andreas; Steiner, Thomas (2018). pp.233–234</ref> During his stay in Jena, he was supported by [[Hermann Friedrich Teichmeyer]], who lectured at the faculty of medicine.<ref name=":1">Kleinert, Andreas; Steiner, Thomas (2018). p.234</ref> In October 1729, he graduated under Simon Paul Hirscher from the faculty of medicine.<ref name=":1" /> Following he returned to Pressburg where he worked as a medic until December 1731.<ref name=":1" /> Following he worked temporarily as the city [[physician]] in Debrecen until early 1732.<ref name=":0" /> In 1732 he returned to Jena where he requested a degree from the faculty of philosophy and also the possibility to give lectures in the faculty of philosophy.<ref name=":1" /> He graduated in May 1732 he began to lecture in 1733. In September the same year he was nominated a professor in the faculty of philosophy where he soon lectured the metaphysics of [[Christian Wolff (philosopher)|Christian Wolff]].<ref name=":1" />

== University of Göttingen ==
The university in Göttingen was established after a visit by [[George II of Great Britain|George II]] to [[Hanover]] in 1732.<ref name=":2">Kleinert, Andreas; Steiner, Thomas (2018). p.235</ref> After Hamberger was denied his resignation from the University of Jena, he suggested von Segner instead.<ref name=":2" /> 1735 Segner became the professor of mathematics and physics at the [[University of Göttingen]].<ref name=":2" /> As in January 1736 the professor for medicine died, he also lectured in the faculty of medicine.<ref name=":2" />

== University of Halle ==
After [[Christian Wolff (philosopher)|Christian Wolff]] died, the Prussian King [[Frederick the Great|Friedrich II]] requested from the mathematician [[Leonhard Euler]] advice on who could be succeed Wolff at the [[Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg|University of Halle]].<ref name=":3">Kleinert, Andreas; Steiner, Thomas (2018). pp.244–245</ref> Euler suggested [[Daniel Bernoulli]] who did not accept.<ref name=":3" /> Then Euler suggested von Segner, who requested the recognition of his Hungarian title and an extraordinary treatment at the university in return of his acceptance.<ref name=":3" /> In 1755 he became a professor at Halle, where he divided the lectures in mathematics and physics with [[Johann Joachim Lange]].<ref>Kleinert, Andreas; Steiner, Thomas (2018). pp.245–246</ref> In Halle he also established an observatory. Von Segner died on the 5 October 1777.<ref>Kleinert, Andreas; Steiner, Thomas (2018). p.254</ref>

==Connections==
One of the best-known scientists of his age, Segner was a member of the academies of [[Prussian Academy of Sciences|Berlin]], [[Royal Society|London]], and [[Russian Academy of Sciences|Saint Petersburg]]. According to [[Mathematics Genealogy Project]], [[as of]] February 2013, he has over 66 thousand [[Academic genealogy|academic descendants]], out of the total 170 thousand mathematicians in the database.

==Contributions==
He was the first scientist to use the reactive force of water and constructed the first water-jet, the [[Segner wheel]], which resembles one type of modern [[Irrigation sprinkler|lawn sprinkler]]. Segner, also produced the first proof of [[Descartes' rule of signs]]. Historians of science remember him as the father of the [[water turbine]]. The lunar crater [[Segner (crater)|Segner]] is named after him, as is asteroid [[28878 Segner]].

== Personal life ==
In 1732, he married Carolina Sophia, the daughter of Hermann Friedrich Teichmeier.<ref name=":1" /> They had three children<ref name=":1" /> of which two reached adulthood.<ref name=":1" />
